paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Water bears, or tardigrades, are microscopic animals, rarely longer than half a millimetre, that live in moss, lichen, soil and the sediments of lakes and oceans across the planet. They were first described in 1773 by a German pastor, Johann August Ephraim Goeze, who called them 'little water bears' because of the slow, lumbering way they walk on their eight stubby legs. A few years later, the Italian biologist Lazzaro Spallanzani gave them the scientific name Tardigrada, meaning 'slow steppers'. Today, around 1,300 species have been identified.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What makes tardigrades remarkable is not their appearance but their resilience. When their environment dries up, they can pull in their head and legs, expel almost all of the water from their bodies and enter a state known as cryptobiosis. In this condition, they form a shrivelled, barrel-shaped structure called a tun, and their metabolism drops to less than 0.01 per cent of its normal rate. Tuns have been brought back to life after many years in dry storage, simply by adding water.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Tardigrades in this state can withstand conditions that would kill most other animals. Experiments have shown that they can survive temperatures as low as minus 272 degrees Celsius, close to absolute zero, and as high as around 150 degrees for short periods. They can also tolerate pressures six times greater than those found in the deepest part of the ocean, and doses of radiation hundreds of times higher than would kill a human. In 2007, a team of European scientists attached dried tardigrades to the outside of a spacecraft and exposed them to the vacuum of space and to solar radiation for ten days. When the animals returned to Earth and were rehydrated, a number of them revived, and some even laid eggs that hatched.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For many years, scientists did not know how tardigrades protect themselves. In 2016, researchers in Japan studying the species Ramazzottius varieornatus discovered a protein, which they named Dsup, short for 'damage suppressor', that appears to shield the animal's DNA from radiation damage. When the researchers inserted the gene for this protein into human cells in a laboratory, the cells became around forty per cent more resistant to X-rays. Other researchers have since found that tardigrades produce sugars and unusual proteins that turn into a glass-like substance as the animal dries out, supporting the structures inside its cells.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These discoveries have raised hopes of practical applications. One possibility is in medicine: vaccines and some medicines must be kept cold during transport, which is expensive and difficult in remote regions. If scientists can copy the way tardigrades preserve their cells, it may be possible to store such products at room temperature. Others suggest that Dsup might one day protect cancer patients from the side effects of radiotherapy, or astronauts from cosmic radiation on long missions. However, most of this research is still at an early stage, and it is not yet clear how well the protein would work in a living human body rather than in cells in a laboratory dish.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It is also worth remembering that tardigrades are not indestructible. Most of the time, they live active lives in thin films of water around moss, and in that state they are as vulnerable as any other small animal. Their extraordinary toughness applies only when they are dried out, and even then they can die if they stay dry for too long. Some scientists also point out that survival in space is of limited importance, because it is not something tardigrades would ever meet naturally. Their toughness is more likely an adaptation to the unpredictable conditions in the places where they actually live, such as mosses that frequently dry out in summer.
